title: Memory
summary: Anonymous and shared mappings, protection changes and the faults they produce, the program break and memory locking behave as POSIX requires, on every target.

cases.title: An anonymous MAP_PRIVATE mapping of 16 pages reads as zero throughout and keeps what is written to every page
An anonymous MAP_SHARED mapping of 16 pages reads as zero throughout and keeps what is written to every page
mmap returns a page-aligned address for lengths of 1, 4095, 4096 and 4097 bytes
Linux policy: a mapping whose length is not a multiple of the page size covers the whole last page: its last byte reads zero and can be written
Two anonymous mappings made one after the other do not overlap, and writing one leaves the other unchanged
mmap without MAP_FIXED, given a hint inside an existing mapping, places the new mapping elsewhere and leaves the existing one unchanged
Linux policy: mmap without MAP_FIXED uses a free, page-aligned hint address exactly
MAP_FIXED over the middle page of a 3-page mapping replaces it with a zero-filled page at exactly that address and leaves the pages either side unchanged
MAP_FIXED at an address that is not page-aligned fails with EINVAL and leaves the mapping there unchanged
Linux ABI: MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE at an address already mapped fails with EEXIST and leaves that mapping unchanged
Linux ABI: MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE at a free page-aligned address maps exactly there
mmap of length 0 fails with EINVAL
mmap with neither MAP_SHARED nor MAP_PRIVATE fails with EINVAL
mmap of a file at an offset that is not a multiple of the page size fails with EINVAL
mmap without MAP_ANONYMOUS of descriptor -1 or of a closed descriptor fails with EBADF
mmap of 2^60 bytes, more address space than a process has, fails with ENOMEM
MAP_FIXED at 2^56, past the end of the user address space, fails with ENOMEM or EINVAL
With RLIMIT_AS at 256 MiB, a 512 MiB mmap that succeeds without the limit fails with ENOMEM, and a 16 MiB one succeeds
After munmap, every page of the former mapping raises SIGSEGV with SEGV_MAPERR and si_addr the byte touched
munmap of the middle page of a 3-page mapping splits it: the outer pages keep their contents and the middle one raises SEGV_MAPERR
munmap of the first and last pages of a 4-page mapping leaves the middle two with their contents and the ends unmapped
munmap of a page-aligned range with nothing mapped in it succeeds
One munmap across two separate mappings and the gap between them removes both
munmap at an address that is not page-aligned fails with EINVAL and leaves the mapping in place
munmap of length 0 fails with EINVAL
A page mapped with MAP_FIXED into the hole a munmap left reads as zero, not the old contents
Linux policy: touching one byte every 1 MiB of a 256 MiB anonymous mapping makes about 256 pages resident, not 65536
Each page of a 16 MiB anonymous mapping, touched in order, keeps its own contents, and unmapping it gives back all 4096 pages as resident
Mapping, touching and unmapping 1 MiB 100 times leaves free memory within 4 MiB of where it was and the resident set no larger
1000 one-page anonymous mappings exist at once at distinct addresses, each keeping its own contents, and all unmap

With two to four processors, worker threads pinned one to each other processor and reading a page the case's thread has just unmapped raise SIGSEGV with SEGV_MAPERR at the byte read every time and never read the old page
Reading a PROT_NONE mapping raises SIGSEGV with SEGV_ACCERR and si_addr the byte read
Writing a PROT_NONE mapping raises SIGSEGV with SEGV_ACCERR and si_addr the byte written
Writing a PROT_READ mapping raises SIGSEGV with SEGV_ACCERR and leaves the byte unchanged, while reading succeeds
Reading an address with nothing mapped raises SIGSEGV with SEGV_MAPERR and si_addr that address
A SIGSEGV handler that mprotects the faulting page writable and returns lets the write complete: 64 PROT_NONE pages take exactly 64 faults, each SEGV_ACCERR at the byte written
mprotect to PROT_READ keeps the contents readable and makes writes raise SEGV_ACCERR
mprotect to PROT_READ makes writes raise SEGV_ACCERR, and mprotect back to PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE lets writes succeed and keeps the contents
mprotect to PROT_NONE and back to PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE keeps the contents, and reads fault in between
A PROT_NONE guard page in the middle of a mapping faults at its first and last bytes while the bytes either side stay accessible
mprotect of the first page of a 4-page mapping to PROT_READ changes only that page
mprotect of two middle pages of a 6-page mapping to PROT_READ makes both refuse writes, and mprotect of one of them back leaves exactly the other read-only
mprotect at an address that is not page-aligned fails with EINVAL and leaves the protection unchanged
mprotect of a range that includes an unmapped page fails with ENOMEM
Linux ABI: mprotect with an unknown protection bit fails with EINVAL
mprotect adding PROT_WRITE to a MAP_SHARED mapping of a file opened read-only fails with EACCES
Linux policy: calling into a PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE anonymous mapping raises SIGSEGV with SEGV_ACCERR at the call's target (ARM64 and x86-64 both enforce no-execute)
Code in a file mapped PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC runs, and after mprotect to PROT_READ calling it raises SIGSEGV with SEGV_ACCERR
Calling code in a file mapped PROT_READ raises SIGSEGV, and after mprotect adds PROT_EXEC the code runs
Linux ABI: code written into an anonymous mapping and made coherent as a C library's __clear_cache does (ARM64 DC CVAU and IC IVAU from user mode) runs after mprotect to PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC
A forked child inherits each page's protection: its PROT_NONE page raises SEGV_ACCERR at the byte read, and its PROT_READ page raises SEGV_ACCERR at the byte written but reads
With two to four processors, a write by a worker thread pinned to another processor, begun after mprotect to PROT_READ returned, always raises SIGSEGV with SEGV_ACCERR at the byte written
A MAP_SHARED anonymous page written by the parent after fork is seen by the child
A MAP_SHARED anonymous page written by the child is seen by the parent
Parent and child take 100 turns storing to a MAP_SHARED anonymous page, each seeing the other's latest store
Two processes each atomically adding 1 to a counter in a MAP_SHARED anonymous page 100000 times leave 200000
After fork, a child's stores to a MAP_PRIVATE anonymous page are not seen by the parent
After fork, the parent's stores to a MAP_PRIVATE anonymous page are not seen by the child
After fork, parent and child each rewrite all 64 pages of a MAP_PRIVATE mapping and each sees only its own stores
A child's store into a MAP_SHARED file mapping inherited across fork is seen through the parent's mapping and by read()
Two processes that each map the same file MAP_SHARED see each other's stores
Stores into a MAP_SHARED mapping of a sparse file are on disk when msync(MS_SYNC) returns: the file has the disk blocks they need (st_blocks), and read() returns them
A write() to a file is seen at once through an existing MAP_SHARED mapping of it
Stores into a MAP_PRIVATE file mapping are not written to the file and not seen by another process's MAP_SHARED mapping of it
A child's munmap of an inherited MAP_SHARED anonymous mapping makes its own reads raise SEGV_MAPERR at the byte read, and leaves the parent's view, and its later stores, in place
After the parent unmaps a MAP_SHARED anonymous mapping, the child still reads the parent's last store and can store its own
The part of a file mapping's last page past the end of the file reads as zero, and a store there is never written to the file: the file stays 100 bytes and, extended afterwards, reads zero there
Touching a page of a file mapping that lies wholly past the end of the file raises SIGBUS with BUS_ADRERR or BUS_OBJERR and si_addr the byte touched
Linux policy: after the file is truncated, touching a page of its MAP_SHARED mapping past the new end raises SIGBUS with BUS_ADRERR or BUS_OBJERR at the byte touched
mmap of a file opened O_WRONLY fails with EACCES
mmap with PROT_WRITE and MAP_SHARED of a file opened O_RDONLY fails with EACCES
mmap with PROT_WRITE and MAP_PRIVATE of a file opened O_RDONLY succeeds, and its stores stay private
Linux policy: mmap of a pipe fails with ENODEV
brk(0), as a C library's sbrk(0) makes it, reports the same nonzero break each time
Growing the break by 64 KiB succeeds, and the new memory reads as zero and keeps what is written
Linux ABI: brk sets and returns exactly the break asked for, not one rounded up to a page
Successive sbrk(4096) calls return consecutive blocks, each starting at the previous break
Shrinking the break with sbrk(-8192) moves it down, and touching memory above the new break raises SIGSEGV with SEGV_MAPERR
Linux policy: memory given back by shrinking the break and then regrown reads as zero, not the old contents
brk below the start of the heap fails and leaves the break unchanged
Linux policy: growing the break by 1 TiB fails and leaves the break unchanged
With RLIMIT_DATA at 0, growing the break fails and leaves it unchanged; with the limit raised again the same growth succeeds
Linux policy: with RLIMIT_DATA at 0, a private writable anonymous mmap fails with ENOMEM while a read-only one succeeds
A forked child inherits the break and the heap's contents, and its brk leaves the parent's break unchanged
Growing the break by 8 MiB gives 2048 pages that each keep their own index, and touching them makes 2048 to 2112 more pages resident
mlock of 16 untouched anonymous pages succeeds and makes them resident: unmapping them gives back all 16 as resident pages
munlock of a locked range succeeds, unlocks it (VmLck falls back by the 16 kB mlock added) and leaves its contents unchanged
Linux policy: mlock and munlock of 10 bytes inside a page lock and unlock that whole page (VmLck changes by 4 kB)
mlock of a range that includes an unmapped page fails with ENOMEM
munlock of a range that includes an unmapped page fails with ENOMEM
Linux policy: an unprivileged process with RLIMIT_MEMLOCK at 0 is refused mlock with EPERM
Linux policy: an unprivileged process may lock 32 KiB under a 64 KiB RLIMIT_MEMLOCK and is refused 64 KiB more with ENOMEM
mlockall(MCL_CURRENT) makes an untouched mapping that existed before it resident: unmapping it gives back all 16 pages as resident
After mlockall(MCL_FUTURE), a new anonymous mapping is resident as soon as mmap returns: unmapping it untouched gives back all 16 pages as resident
mlockall with no flags or with an unknown flag fails with EINVAL
munlockall succeeds whether or not anything is locked, brings VmLck to 0 after an mlock, and leaves contents unchanged
msync(MS_ASYNC) of a MAP_SHARED file mapping returns 0 and read() returns the stores made through it
msync(MS_SYNC|MS_INVALIDATE) of a MAP_SHARED file mapping returns 0, and the mapping shows a write() made to the file
msync with both MS_SYNC and MS_ASYNC fails with EINVAL
msync with an unknown flag fails with EINVAL
msync at an address that is not page-aligned fails with EINVAL
msync of a range that includes an unmapped page fails with ENOMEM
msync(MS_SYNC|MS_INVALIDATE) of a range locked by mlock fails with EBUSY
Linux policy: msync(MS_SYNC) of an anonymous mapping returns 0
posix_madvise with POSIX_MADV_NORMAL, SEQUENTIAL, RANDOM and WILLNEED returns 0 and leaves the contents unchanged
posix_madvise with an unknown advice value returns EINVAL
posix_madvise of a range that includes an unmapped page returns ENOMEM
Linux policy: posix_madvise at an address that is not page-aligned returns EINVAL
Linux ABI: madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) of private anonymous memory frees its pages, which then read as zero
Linux ABI: mincore reports the touched pages of an anonymous mapping resident and the untouched ones not
Linux ABI: mincore of a range that includes an unmapped page fails with ENOMEM
Linux ABI: mincore at an address that is not page-aligned fails with EINVAL
